# Fitness plan — return to running after a layoff

*Fictional illustration of [`templates/fitness-plan.md`](../../templates/fitness-plan.md). Not a plan
for any real person, and not guidance to anyone.*

Sixteen weeks, for someone returning to running after roughly a year away.

## Goals

**Leading goal:** run 10 km continuously at conversational pace, within sixteen weeks.

Measured by: completing the distance able to speak in full sentences throughout. Not by time — pace
targets at this stage would push intensity up and volume tolerance is the constraint.

**Secondary, conceding to the above:** maintain the strength work already being done twice weekly.
Where the two compete for recovery, running leads and a strength session is dropped rather than a run
— for the first eight weeks, when tissue tolerance is the limiting factor. After that they are
balanced again.

**Not a goal:** body composition change. Pursuing it simultaneously would put this person in a
deficit during the period when connective tissue needs to adapt, which is the wrong trade.

## Baseline

**Current capacity.** Can run about 10 minutes continuously at an easy effort before form degrades.
Walks 30–40 minutes most days without difficulty. Two strength sessions weekly, sustained for six
months, with no interruption during the running layoff.

**History.** Ran regularly for four years until about twelve months ago; had reached 10 km
comfortably and a half marathon once. Stopped for reasons unrelated to injury.

This history is the important part of this baseline and the reason the plan is conservative. Aerobic
fitness returns faster than tendon and bone tolerance, and the combination of a beginner's tissue
readiness with a trained person's technique and confidence is where returning runners get hurt. The
danger here is that week six will feel far too easy.

**Constraints.** No current injuries. Previous mild Achilles irritation about three years ago,
resolved, no recurrence. Three to four sessions weekly is what the schedule allows. Access to
outdoor routes and a gym.

## Progression

**What increases:** running volume only, for the first eight weeks. Intensity stays at easy
throughout that period. One variable at a time.

**By how much:** total weekly running time increases by no more than about 10% per week, with a
lighter week every fourth week at roughly 60% of the preceding week.

**On what trigger:** the previous week was completed as prescribed, at conversational effort, with no
knee, shin, or Achilles symptoms persisting into the following day.

**When the trigger is not met:** repeat the week rather than advancing. If it is not met twice in a
row, reduce to the last comfortably completed week and reassess whether something outside training
has changed — sleep, work, or life load.

Weeks 9–16 add one faster session weekly, at which point running volume holds steady. Intensity and
volume do not increase in the same week at any point.

## Recovery and Rest

**Rest days:** at least two full non-running days weekly, and never two consecutive running days
before week 6.

**Lighter weeks:** every fourth week, at about 60% of the preceding week's volume. These are in the
plan from the start, not added when something starts to hurt.

**Easy means easy.** Conversational pace, able to speak in full sentences. The most common way a plan
like this fails is that easy days drift up and become moderate — tiring enough to impair recovery,
not hard enough to drive adaptation.

**Signals that recovery is not keeping pace**, read together: resting heart rate elevated against
this person's own baseline for several days, sleep worsening despite adequate opportunity, sessions
feeling harder at unchanged paces, accumulating minor niggles, unusual persistent fatigue.

**Response:** cut the week to the previous lighter week's volume. Not push through. If the signals
persist after a lighter week, reassess the baseline rather than resuming the schedule.

## Pain and Injury Response

**Training discomfort** — diffuse, in the working muscles, eases when effort stops, movement stays
normal. Continue.

**Injury pain** — sharp, localised, often at a joint or tendon, may persist after stopping or worsen
with continued use, alters how you move. **Stop the session.** Not "ease off": stop.

Given this person's history, the specific one to watch is Achilles or heel pain in the morning after
a run.

**After stopping:** do not run for at least 48 hours. Return only if it is symptom-free at rest and
during a short walk. If it recurs on the first return run, stop again and get it assessed rather than
attempting a third time.

**Cross-training remains available** while a specific movement is painful — cycling, swimming,
upper-body work. Stopping running is not stopping training, which is what makes this rule
followable.

**Get it assessed** rather than self-managing if: pain follows a distinct traumatic moment, you
cannot bear weight, there is marked swelling, numbness or weakness, the joint gives way, it wakes you
at night, or it is not improving after about a week of not aggravating it.

## Review Cadence

**Every four weeks**, at the end of each lighter week.

**Assessed on:** whether the prescribed volume was completed, effort at a given pace, resting heart
rate against baseline, sleep, any accumulating niggles, and how the sessions felt across the block —
not the last run. A single bad session reflects sleep, food, stress, heat, and where in the week it
fell at least as much as it reflects fitness.

**Adjustments are proportionate.** A block that went well continues. A block that did not gets one
change, not a rewrite — usually holding volume rather than reducing it.

**At week 8**, an explicit check on whether 10 km by week 16 is still realistic on the evidence. If
the safe rate of progression will not reach it, the date moves. It will not be reached by compressing
the remaining weeks.
